To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

“ERP success is dependent on the CIO and the IT function being able to deliver a high quality IT service, which is aligned to the business strategy, and is seen as an important contributor to business value”.
“ERP implementations that are led effectively by the CIO, and that involve IT in a business partnership role, are more likely to succeed than those that are not.”

the most critical factors in ERP success are: (1) the CIO and senior business executives have a shared vision and strategy; (2) the CIO has the authority and resources to manage the project effectively; and (3) the CIO is able to manage and motivate the business users and their managers to participate in the implementation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the CIO in ERP, and the role of IT in ERP implementations.
the role of the CIO (and IT) in ERP implementation and success.
the roles and responsibilities of the CIO in ERP implementations, and how these roles can be made more effective.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
“ERP is a technology that has been implemented in the wrong way, by the wrong people, for the wrong reasons, with the wrong objectives, and with the wrong expectations.”
the CIO and the IT function should not be asleep at the wheel, and indeed that it is the CIO who must be awake, and driving the car, on ERP and all other major IT projects.

the CIO and it function must take the lead in ensuring that: • The business case is well understood and the benefits and risks are well articulated • The business case, benefits, and risks are clearly communicated throughout the organization • The business and IT teams are integrated and work together • The business is fully engaged and committed to the project • Business process reengineering is undertaken and business process change is well managed
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the IT function must be seen as a strategic asset, not a cost center.
the IT function needs to be more closely aligned with the business, to be more business-oriented, and to have a stronger business focus.
ERP is not a technology, it’s a business process.
The main takeaway from our work is that

ERP, and indeed other large-scale and complex IT projects, require a different style and approach to IT management, and that this must be understood and applied by the CIO and the IT function if they are to be successful.
there is still an IT management crisis in many organizations, and it is not confined to IT projects.
, in the absence of a CIO or IT function with effective capabilities, ERP implementation success will be elusive and its business value will not be realized.
